summary: Screw-pile light at the mouth of the Roanoke River on Albemarle Sound, first lit 1867; the 1887 house was moved to Edenton and opened in 2014.

lens.where: Edenton; sources differ on who holds the lens

structures.note: Lit January 1867; damaged by fire 1885; ice collapse January 1886; the old station was removed (cite 2, 4).
Built 1887 per the Commission and LHF; USLHS and NPS give 1903 for the tower (cite 1, 3).

access.note: Open to the public since 15 August 2014 (LHF). LHF lists visiting hours of Tuesday to Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

facts.agency: Edenton Historical Commission (bought 2007, per the Commission); LHF lists the N.C. Department of Cultural Resources as owner

events.note: Congress appropriated $10,000 for a light vessel at the river mouth (Commission); LHF gives 30 June 1834.
Lightship MM placed at the mouth of the Roanoke River. NPS gives 1835 as the year the station was established.
Confederates held the lightship; Commission says until Union forces took Plymouth in late March 1864. LHF dates the seizure to the 1862 Union invasion.

Lightship scuttled about 40 miles up the river by the Confederates (Commission). The Commission places this in the war years and after the 1864 capture of Plymouth; the year is inferred from its sequence. The 1927 Bulletin list (cite 13) records the lightship as replaced by the Roanoke River lighthouse, without a date.
One-and-a-half-story screw-pile lighthouse built at the river mouth (Commission).
Original fourth-order Fresnel lens installed (USLHS).
First lit January 1867, whale oil (Commission).
Fire at the station in March 1885. The Commission says it damaged the structure; LHF says it destroyed it on 21 March 1885.
Ice on Albemarle Sound cut the pilings in February 1885 (Commission).
Ice severed two of the house's legs in January 1886 and the house fell into the Sound (LHF).
Replacement house authorized in 1886 and built in 1887 (Commission). LHF gives completion and keepers' occupancy on 12 February 1887.
USLHS gives 1903 as the year the tower was established; NPS gives 1903 as the year the light was first lit. Conflicts with 1887 (see notes).
Keeper and assistant keeper towed a disabled motor boat with four people aboard to safety, 8 May 1914.

September 1913 Bulletin reports a recent storm in the vicinity of the North Carolina sounds and lists the Roanoke River light among the structures damaged in Albemarle Sound; the index files it as 'damaged by 1913 hurricane' (p. 82).
Keeper and assistant helped float the schooner W. H. French, 27 July 1917.
Assistant keeper floated the launch Laum, 16 March 1920.
Keeper helped rescue men adrift in a disabled launch, February 1921 (OCR day garbled).
Keepers' service ended with the 1933 roster; LHF says the light was discontinued on 29 June 1933.
Light discontinued and deactivated by the Coast Guard.
Coast Guard sold the house and two other sound lights to Elijah Tate for $10 each.
House moved across Albemarle Sound from the river mouth to Filberts Creek, west of Edenton (NPS: moved 1955).
Emmett Wiggins's primary residence from about 1960 until his death in 1995 (LHF, Commission).
Edenton Historical Commission bought the house for $225,000 and moved it to Colonial Park, 23 May 2007.
Exterior restoration June to October 2010 (LHF).
Moved onto a new foundation of pilings in the harbor, 1 May 2012 (LHF).
Opened to the public 15 August 2014 after interior restoration (LHF).

corrections.why: The record point is the surviving house on the Edenton waterfront, where it has stood since 1955 and again since 2007. The station stood at the river mouth in Albemarle Sound until 1955. USLHS gives 35 deg 56.58 min N, 76 deg 41.42 min W (minute precision). Check before using.
USLHS gives the height of light above mean high water as 40 feet (12.2 m); NPS gives a focal plane of 35 feet (10.7 m). No source read supports 3.7 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata's 1867 is the first screw-pile light, first lit January 1867 (Commission). USLHS's 1887 is the replacement house. The first lens year of 1866 (USLHS) belongs to the first house. The record's 1887 'built' entry is the replacement.
NPS gives a focal plane of 35 feet; USLHS gives 40 feet above mean high water. The two may measure different points, so the record uses the USLHS figure with NPS shown in the notes.

notes_for_editor: 1) Lighthouse Board reports for 1866 to 1890 are not in the corpus. The first-light date (1866 or 1867), the 1885 fire and the 1887 rebuilding rest on the Commission and LighthouseFriends (LHF). LHF says it quotes the Board's 1887 report; check that report before publishing the 1887 details. 2) LHF's own dates conflict: it gives a fire on 21 March 1885 and ice in January 1886, but also a fourth-order light 'August 15, 1885' with a temporary lantern. The story follows the 1885 fire and 1886 ice and drops the August 1885 light. 3) The present house: USLHS and NPS give 1903 (tower or first light); the Commission, LHF and the 1887 date in the record give 1887. Unresolved. Wikipedia (not cited) gives 1903 for a second light. 4) Ownership: LHF says the N.C. Department of Cultural Resources owns the house; the Commission says it bought it in 2007. Wikipedia (not cited) names the Town of Edenton. Check the county register. 5) Lens: the Commission says the Coast Guard gave the town a fourth-order lamp; LHF says the lens will return when funded. Status unclear. 6) Keepers before 1899 come from LHF only. USLHS has no head keeper before 1899. Thomas Blount Clifton's 1866 to 1899 tenure needs a primary check. 7) Bulletin OCR: the 1914 keeper name is misprinted; the 1917 schooner name is read as 'W. H. French'; the 1920 launch is named 'Laum' in the OCR; the 1921 day of month is garbled ('February 2.13'). Check the page images before publishing those names and dates. 8) An unrelated Bulletin 1921 item (page 200 of the printed volume, PDF p. 39) names a 'W. B. Clifton' near Detroit River Light; the index entry 'Clifton, W.B., keeper Roanoke River, assists launch 199' may have been misattributed. Not used. 9) The record's 'focal_height_m' 3.7 looks wrong (see corrections). 10) LHF's 'discontinued 29 June 1933' versus 1941 on USLHS, NPS and the Commission is a real conflict; the story gives both. 11) Emmett Wiggins (1921 to 1995, per the Commission) is named because he is deceased and published sources name him in his public role as owner. No family members are named. 12) Photos: the record's Wikimedia photo has no licence and is not added. 13) The Plymouth replica is the record's us-nc-roanoke-river-2 and is not written up here. 14) Verification pass (2026-10-28): the September 1913 Bulletin (PDF p. 34) lists 'Wade Point and Roanoke River in Albemarle Sound' among damaged structures, and the Bulletin's text says 'recent storm in the vicinity of the North Carolina sounds'; the word 'hurricane' is from the index only. The event note no longer gives a storm date (2-3 September), which was not in any source read. 15) The 1914 Bulletin's 'driven ashore and lost' line and the 1920 'J. W. Cooper, assistant keeper, Roanoke River Light Station, N. C.' line were checked against the corpus text. 16) LHF's introduction gives 1941 for discontinuance as well as its 29 June 1933 date; the story reports both.
